issues.legal_issue: An appellate judgment reversing dismissal of a suit must clearly specify the relief granted so that the decree can conform to the judgment.
material_facts: The trial court dismissed a suit seeking multiple forms of relief, and the dismissal was upheld on first appeal.
The High Court allowed the second appeal but stated only that the appeal was allowed, without specifying which reliefs the plaintiffs were entitled to.
The trial court treated the High Court’s direction to prepare a decree as allowing all the reliefs claimed in the plaint.
issues.conclusion: The appellate judgment was insufficiently clear: it should have specified the extent and manner of relief granted. The trial court’s order drawing up a decree on the assumption that all pleaded reliefs had been allowed was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Order VII Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires the plaintiff to state the relief claimed; Order XX requires the judgment to state the relief allowed and the decree to agree with the judgment and specify clearly the relief granted or other determination; and Order XLI Rule 31 requires an appellate judgment reversing or varying a decree to state the relief to which the appellant is entitled. A bare statement that an appeal is allowed, without specifying the relief, fails to discharge that obligation.

predicates.appeal_reverses_suit_dismissal: An appellate court reverses the dismissal of a suit.
predicates.appellate_judgment_omits_specific_relief: The appellate judgment does not identify the relief granted to the successful party.

issues.definition: When an appellate court reverses a suit dismissal but its judgment omits the specific relief granted, the judgment must specify that relief.

issues.legal_issue: An accidental omission to express intended relief in a judgment may be corrected so that the judgment records the court’s intention and a conforming decree can be drawn.
material_facts: The High Court’s judgment showed that it intended the plaintiffs to succeed, but did not state the relief to which they were entitled.
The trial court had prepared a decree referring only to costs and later proposed to prepare a decree granting all the reliefs claimed in the plaint.
The Supreme Court held that the parties could seek rectification of the High Court judgment and that the decree should be drawn after the operative part was clarified.
issues.conclusion: The parties were permitted to apply to the High Court under Section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure to rectify the judgment by specifying the relief intended to be granted. Once rectified, a decree could be drawn by the High Court itself, subject to any applicable rules allowing the trial court to perform the ministerial act of drawing it up.
issues.legal_principle: Section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits correction of clerical or arithmetical mistakes and errors arising from accidental slip or omission. It enables a court to amend its judgment to give effect to its meaning and intention. In re Swire; Mellor v. Swire, (1885) 30 Ch. D. 239, supports the court’s power to make its record express the order actually intended, subject to avoiding injustice or imposing terms that preclude it.

predicates.civil_suit_appeal: The matter arises from an appeal in a civil suit.
predicates.judgment_shows_intended_success: The judgment indicates that the court intended the successful party to prevail.
predicates.judgment_accidentally_omits_intended_rel: The judgment omits the relief intended to be granted because of an accidental slip or omission.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal judgment indicates intended success but accidentally omits the intended relief, the judgment may be rectified to express that relief.
